title: Arrays and strings
sub: The length inside the object, the terminator and the cost of small strings
cards/0/title: An array: the length before the elements
cards/0/body:
An array is a variable-size object. After the type pointer comes the length: a 4-byte int and, on x64, 4 more bytes of padding. Right after them come the elements, back to back, with no gaps.

  • new byte[0] — 24 bytes: header, type, length;
  • new byte[10] — 24 + 10 = 34 → 40;
  • new int[4] — 24 + 16 = 40;
  • new object[3] — 24 + 3 × 8 = 48: the slots hold references, the objects themselves live elsewhere.

The element type is not stored in the object: int[] and string[] have their own MethodTables, and the element size (ComponentSize) is recorded there too.
cards/0/deep: In the runtime this is ArrayBase from object.h: the m_NumComponents field and, on a 64-bit platform, pad. The length is 32-bit, so there are at most Array.MaxLength elements (2,147,483,591, .NET 6+). The array can still exceed 2 GB in bytes: modern .NET allows large objects on 64-bit by default, while .NET Framework needed gcAllowVeryLargeObjects.
cards/1/q: How many bytes does new long[3] take on x64?
cards/1/explain: 24 bytes of bookkeeping (header, type, length with padding) plus 3 × 8 bytes of elements — 48.
cards/1/wrong/1: That is 16 + 24: you forgot the 8 bytes for the length.
cards/1/wrong/2: The elements live inside the array object, not separately.
cards/2/body:
int[2, 3] is one object. After the total length (6) it stores the length of each dimension and the lower bounds, and then all 6 elements back to back, row by row. In total 16 + 8 + 8 + 8 + 24 = 64 bytes.

int[2][] with two rows of 3 is three objects: an outer array of references (40 bytes) and two 40-byte arrays somewhere in the heap. 120 bytes in total, plus an extra hop through a reference on every access.
cards/2/code:
var grid = new int[2, 3];   // 1 object, 64 bytes

var rows = new int[2][];    // 40 bytes: two references
rows[0] = new int[3];       // + 40 bytes
rows[1] = new int[3];       // + 40 bytes
cards/2/deep: A one-dimensional array with a zero lower bound (an SZ array in CLR terms) has its own IL instructions ldelem/stelem, and in simple loops the JIT often removes the bounds check. Access to a multidimensional array goes through the array type's Get/Set/Address methods; since .NET 7 the JIT expands them into direct code, but every index is still checked against its lower bound.
cards/3/q: Match the expression to the object size on x64
cards/4/title: A string: length, characters and a zero at the end
cards/4/body:
A string also keeps its length inside: after the type pointer there is an int with the character count, followed by the UTF-16 characters, 2 bytes each. And after the last character the CLR puts one more: the null terminator '\0'. It is not counted in Length.

The base size of a string is 8 + 8 + 4 + 2 = 22 bytes (header, type, length, terminator). Then 2 bytes per character and rounding to 8:

  • "a" — 22 + 2 = 24;
  • "abc" — 22 + 6 = 28 → 32;
  • "hello" — 22 + 10 = 32.
cards/4/deep: In the runtime this is StringObject: the fields m_StringLength and m_FirstChar. Strings and arrays are the only variable-size objects: their MethodTable has a non-zero ComponentSize. A string in memory is always UTF-16. A UTF-8 literal "..."u8 from C# 11 is not a string but a ReadOnlySpan<byte> over data in the assembly itself; it creates no heap object.
cards/5/q: How many heap bytes does new string('x', 0) allocate?
cards/5/explain: For a zero length the constructor returns the ready-made empty string and allocates nothing. Likewise Substring(0) and ToString() on a string return the string itself.
cards/5/wrong/2: That is what an empty string would weigh if one were actually created. But there is only one empty string in the process.
cards/6/body:
Let us count a million distinct strings of 10 Latin characters — keys from a file, say.

  • each string: 22 + 20 = 42 → 48 bytes;
  • a million strings — 48 MB;
  • a string[] holding them — another 8 MB of references.

The useful text is 10 MB in ASCII. The rest is UTF-16 (twice the bytes for Latin text), the bookkeeping of every object and alignment. With millions of strings this is where most of the memory goes. Remedies: do not keep several copies of equal strings, store data as UTF-8 in a byte[], parse input through Span<char> without creating substrings.
cards/6/deep: For deduplication, use your own pool on a HashSet<string> or a Dictionary with lookup by ReadOnlySpan<char> via GetAlternateLookup (.NET 9): a string is created only if there is no such one yet. string.Intern is worse for this: interned strings live until the process ends.
cards/7/q: Roughly how much memory does a string[] with a million distinct 10-character strings take?
cards/7/explain: Each string is 48 bytes (22 + 20, rounded to 8), a million strings is 48 MB, plus 8 MB of references in the array.
cards/7/wrong/1: That is just the characters in UTF-16. You forgot the bookkeeping of every string and the array of references.
cards/7/wrong/2: That is what the text would weigh in a single-byte encoding without a single object.
cards/8/body:
Native APIs (Win32, libc) expect a string with a zero at the end. Thanks to the terminator .NET can hand them a string without copying: fixed pins the string and gives a pointer to the first character, and a zero already sits after the last one.

The marshaller does the same for LPWStr parameters: it passes a pointer straight into the string if the string does not need to change. The trap: a .NET string may contain '\0' inside — for C# it is an ordinary character, but native code sees the end of the string there.
cards/8/deep: Never write into a string through such a pointer: strings are immutable, and literals are also shared by the whole process (interned). For a buffer that native code will fill, use a char[], a Span<char> from stackalloc, or string.Create.
cards/9/q: Which line allocates a new heap object every time it runs?
cards/9/explain: A literal is created once per process. The empty string is the ready-made string.Empty. Substring(0) and ToString() return the same string. But Substring(1) copies "bc" into a new 32-byte object.
cards/10/q: What is true about arrays and strings in CoreCLR? Select all.
cards/10/options/0: The length is stored inside the object, before the elements
cards/10/options/1: A '\0' sits after the last character of a string, and Length does not count it
cards/10/options/2: int[2, 3] stores the dimension lengths and lower bounds in the object itself
cards/10/options/3: An int[][] with two rows is a single heap object
cards/10/options/4: A string stores its text in UTF-8
cards/10/explain: A jagged array is an outer array of references plus one object per row. The text of a string in memory is always UTF-16.
cards/11/q: Complete the string size formula for x64
cards/11/code:
static long StringSize(int length) =>
    (___ + 2L * length + 7) & ~7L;  // round up to 8
cards/11/explain: 22 = 8 bytes of header + 8 of type pointer + 4 of length + 2 of terminator. For "abc": 22 + 6 = 28 → 32.
